lesson.title: Savoir vs Connaître
lesson.subtitle: Knowing facts and skills (je sais nager) vs being familiar with people and places (je connais Paris).

hook.title: Why French Has Two Verbs for 'To Know': savoir vs. connaître
hook.content: savoir (je sais, cousin of savant/savvy) is for FACTS, CLAUSES, and SKILLS (Je sais où il est, Je sais parler français — with NO word for 'how'!). connaître (je connais, cousin of reconnaissance) is for PEOPLE, PLACES, and NOUNS you are acquainted with (Je connais Marie, Je connais Paris)!

footnotes.title: Why French never translates 'how' in 'I know how to speak'
footnotes.content: savoir chains directly to the bare infinitive with NO 'comment': Je sais nager ('I know [how] to swim')!

pattern.title: Clause or Bare Infinitive → savoir (je sais); Person or Place Noun → connaître (je connais)
pattern.content: Check what follows 'know': a noun takes connaître; a clause, bare infinitive, or nothing at all (Je ne sais pas) takes savoir!
pattern.linguist_note: Latin sapere ('be wise') vs. cognōscere ('be acquainted with') divides propositional knowledge from entity familiarity.
pattern.trap_note: Never say *Je connais où il est or *Je sais Marie — nouns take connais, clauses and infinitives take sais!

exercises.prompt: Match each 'know' sentence with savoir (je sais) or connaître (je connais):

matching_pairs.english: I know Paris very well (place noun)
I know where he is (clause with où)
I know how to speak French (bare infinitive)

exercises.target_answer: Je connais très bien Paris, Je connais ton frère, Je sais où il est, Je sais parler français, Je ne sais pas
exercises.meaning: I know Paris very well (place noun), I know your brother (person noun), I know where he is (clause with où), I know how to speak French (bare infinitive), I don't know (standing alone)
exercises.explanation: connaître always takes a direct noun object; savoir takes clauses, infinitives, or stands alone.

exercises.prompt: French connaître ('to be familiar with') shares its Latin root cognōscere with which English word for a military scouting mission?
exercises.explanation: Reconnaissance is literally 'getting to know (reconnaître) the terrain'.

exercises.prompt: How do you say 'Do you know this restaurant?' vs. 'Do you know where the restaurant is?'
options: Tu connais ce restaurant ? / Tu sais où est le restaurant ?
Tu sais ce restaurant ? / Tu connais où est le restaurant ?
Tu connais ce restaurant ? / Tu connais où est le restaurant ?
exercises.target_answer: Tu connais ce restaurant ? / Tu sais où est le restaurant ?
exercises.meaning: Noun object takes connais; où-clause takes sais
exercises.explanation: ce restaurant is a noun (connais); où est le restaurant is a clause (sais).

exercises.idea: I know your friend and I know where he lives
cues: I know your friend → Je connais ton ami
and I know where he lives → et je sais où il habite
idea_parts: person acquaintance → Je connais ton ami
fact clause → et je sais où il habite
exercises.target_answer: Je connais ton ami et je sais où il habite
exercises.meaning: I know your friend and I know where he lives
exercises.explanation: ton ami (noun) takes connais; où il habite (clause) takes sais.

diagnosis.cue: Use connais before ton ami and sais before où il habite.

exercises.prompt: Listen and write the whole sentence.
exercises.spoken: Je ne sais pas pourquoi il est parti
exercises.target_answer: Je ne sais pas pourquoi il est parti
exercises.meaning: I don't know why he left
exercises.explanation: savoir is used before pourquoi and in Je ne sais pas.
exercises.affirmation: You used Je ne sais pas before pourquoi il est parti.

summary.outcome: Distinguish savoir (facts, clauses, bare infinitives for skills) from connaître (people, places, and noun objects).

use_example.german: Je connais bien cette ville, donc je sais où aller.
use_example.english: I know this city well, so I know where to go.

summary.takeaway: connaître + Noun (people/places); savoir + Clause or Bare Infinitive (facts/skills).
summary.curiosity_teaser: Up next on Le Pont ([28] qui & que): see how Savoir vs Connaître leads directly into qui & que.

twist.prompt: Think it through again without looking back — express "I know your friend and I know where he lives" in French:
twist.target_answer: Je connais ton ami et je sais où il habite
twist.explanation: Re-constructing "Je connais ton ami et je sais où il habite" from the underlying rule cements the pattern of Savoir vs Connaître.

savoir.english_meaning: to know (facts, how to do something)
savoir.etymology_derivation: Used for facts, information, and skills (je sais + infinitive, without 'how').

connaître.english_meaning: to know, be familiar with (people, places)
connaître.etymology_derivation: Always takes a noun object (a person, city, book, or restaurant).

ville.etymology_derivation: Latin vīlla 'country estate' grew into the whole city in French (leaving 'city' as la cité for the historic core).

docteur.etymology_derivation: Latin doctor 'teacher'. -or/-er nouns convert to -eur and are usually masculine.

où.etymology_derivation: Latin ubi 'where' — the root English borrowed wholesale in 'ubiquitous' (present everywhere).

pourquoi.etymology_derivation: pour + quoi = 'for what' — English's 'wherefore' (for-what) built the same way: wherefore art thou.

ami.etymology_derivation: In liaison, un ami sounds like /œ̃.na.mi/ and mes amis like /me.za.mi/.
